opening_message:
Ticket 1: Jason Hansen (employee ID E044) requests admin access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E044.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Engineer (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Jason Hansen (E044) is a full-time Engineer requesting admin access to Payroll. Payroll is owned by the Payroll Specialist role, and Engineers are not that role, so admin is not permitted. Maximum for full-time employees is write. Recommend granting write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Engineer (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security DB shows Jason Hansen (E044) is a contractor with basic security training (HR note said full-time; security record differs). Contractors max at read without advanced training; never admin. Requested admin exceeds max, so recommend granting read.
reason: Jason Hansen (E044) requested admin access to Payroll, which exceeds the maximum allowed under either note. Payroll is owned by the Payroll Specialist role; Jason is an Engineer, so even as a full-time employee admin is not permitted (max write per HR note). The Security note indicates he is a contractor with basic training, whose max is read and who can never have admin. Because the employment-type records conflict, the highest level that complies with both interpretations is read, and read is at or below the maximum in both cases. Granting read is the safe, policy-compliant level.

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket carefully.

Employee: Jason Hansen (E044)
Request: admin access to Payroll

Notes from team memory:
- Note 1 (HR): role Engineer, employment type full_time, recommendation for Payroll: write. Comment: Payroll is owned by Payroll Specialist role; Engineers not that role, so admin not permitted. Max for full-time is write. Recommend write.
- Note 2 (Security): role Engineer, employment type contractor, security training basic, recommendation for Payroll: read. Comment: Security DB says contractor with basic training. Contractors max at read without advanced training; never admin. Requested admin exceeds max, so recommend read.

Discrepancy: HR says full-time, Security says contractor. The two notes conflict on employment type.

The access policy:
1. full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if the employee's role owns the system.
2. contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

Payroll is owned by Payroll Specialist role. Jason is Engineer, so even if full-time, admin is not allowed (only up to write). If contractor, max read (basic training). Either way, admin is not permitted.

Requested admin exceeds max in both cases. So grant the maximum. Which maximum? HR says write; Security says read. Since the requested level is above the maximum, grant the maximum.

But which maximum applies? The notes conflict. Given the conflicting evidence, the safest decision... The policy says never grant more than requested. Requested is admin. Grant maximum allowed. The maximum based on evidence: HR says write, Security says read. Since there's conflicting info, I need to decide.

The security note says security DB shows contractor with basic training; HR said full-time; security record differs. The security agent looked up employment type in own database. HR looked up in own database too.

Hmm. The task says the Approver reads the notes and makes the final decision. I should use the information available. Both notes are from different databases with conflicting employment types. But note 1's role was looked up, employment full-time looked up. Note 2 says role not looked up in own database (same value as note 1), employment type contractor looked up, security training basic looked up.

Given the conflict, what to do? The recommendation of read (from security) is more conservative/restrictive. Granting write when the employee might be a contractor with basic training could violate policy. The safest level consistent with both notes is... Actually both notes agree admin is not allowed. The maximums: full-time writes, contractor read. If we're uncertain, should we grant the lower of the two recommendations? The two recommend write and read.

Given discrepancy, perhaps grant the most restrictive valid level (read) because granting write would violate policy if employee is contractor. Granting read is safe under both: full-time can have read (≤ write), contractor can have read. Read is at or below both maximums. But policy says "If the requested level is above the maximum, grant the maximum." The maximum depends on which is true. Since we can't be certain, granting read is the only level that satisfies both possible statuses and doesn't exceed request.

Actually the decision should be based on the information. I'll go with read, citing the conflict and that read is the highest level permissible under both interpretations, and requesting admin exceeds max.

Let me submit read.
